Systematic optimization of PA coating formation. Effect of solution volume at constant TMC concentration (1 wt%): (a) cycling stability over 10 cycles (1-hour desorption at 100°C per cycle) and (b) time to reach 95% CO capacity under simulated flue gas conditions (15% CO /N , 30°C). 2 2 2 22 a ) a ) b ) b ) T e m p e ra tu re o ( C ) c ) Figure 16a shows cycling stability under accelerated conditions (1-h desorption at 100°C per cycle). TAPA-loaded SBA-15 (uncoated sample) exhibits severe degradation from 2.37 to 1.41 mmol g-1 (40.6% loss). T1-1x shows moderate improvement: 1.40 to 0.90 mmol g-1 (35.7% loss). T1-2x further improves: 1.57 to 1.28 mmol g-1 (18.3% loss). T1-4x shows excellent stability: 1.61 to 1.57 mmol g-1 (only 2.2% loss), an 18-fold improvement. The systematic improvement with increasing solution volume occurs despite all samples having stoichiometric TMC excess (TMC:TAPA ratios of 1.83:1 to 7.33:1), indicating that coating quality is limited by solution distribution rather than chemical availability. This interpretation is directly supported by TGA characterization (Figure 15b), which shows that the PA decomposition features (215-350°C and 400-650°C) increase systematically in intensity with solution volume: T1-1x < T1-2x < T1-4x. The correlation between PA content (TGA) and cycling stability (Figure 16a) confirms that increased solution volume produces more extensive coating coverage. Quantitatively, T1-4x exhibits PA decomposition accounting for approximately 21% of total mass loss compared to only 16.7% for T1-1x, consistent with the 18-fold difference in stability performance. The solution volume dependence likely reflects improved wetting and TMC distribution throughout the heterogeneous particle bed at higher volumes, as interfacial polymerization occurs only where TMC solution contacts TAPA-loaded surfaces.26 Insufficient solution volume may result in incomplete particle wetting or poor penetration into agglomerates, leaving unreacted pore mouths that allow continued amine loss. The progressive improvement from T1-1x to T1-4x confirms that coating uniformity across the particle ensemble, not chemical stoichiometry, limits performance at low solution volumes. The varying initial capacities (1.40-1.61 mmol g-1) despite identical initial amine loading (58.1 wt%) reflect the effects of the coating process on the final CO capture traits of the materials. 2 Reasons for the varying capacities include partial amine loss during coating procedure itself and differing coating quality, leading to amine loss during the sorbent degassing. T1-1x (lower capacity) suggests more amine evaporates before protective coating forms on all particles, consistent with incomplete initial coverage. T1-4x (higher capacity) indicates better amine preservation through rapid, uniform coating formation. However, enhanced stability comes with a kinetic trade-off. Figure 16b shows the time to reach 95% CO capacity under simulated flue gas conditions (15% CO , 30°C). Uncoated reaches 2 2 95% capacity in 6.5 min. T1-1x: 13.7 min (2.1x slower), T1-2x: 15.8 min (2.4x), T1-4x: 18.8 min (2.9x).
